newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal drama far from final chapter.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal drama far from final chapter.

text.p: A Japanese scandal linking financiers, racketeers and possibly politicians is still unfolding with more twists in the plot likely before its final chapter is written.
The affair, which began with admissions of payoffs to racketeers by executives at giant Nomura, is shedding a harsh spotlight on Japan's deep-rooted ties between gangsters and business.

"This looks like it goes to the very core of the matter, and the fact that such dark secrets have started to come out is a sign that the system itself is breaking down," said Yasunori Sone, a political scientist at Keio University.
"There could be moves to prevent everything from coming out, but I don't know if that will be possible."

Another twist in the saga emerged on Friday when Dai-Ichi Kangyo (DKB), one of Japan's biggest banks, said its president, chairman and five advisers would step down to atone for the bank's links to an alleged corporate extortionist, or "sokaiya" suspected of taking illegal payoffs from Nomura.

DKB admitted its inability to cut links to racketeers lay behind the dubious loans. It said the bank might have tried to cover up the deals and added that more revelations of similar misdeeds might lie ahead.

Prosecutors have arrested racketeer Ryuichi Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori and raided Nomura's head office and branches after taking in two former Nomura managing directors and another senior official suspected of breaking the law with payoffs to the "sokaiya."
That investigation is now focusing on whether other top Nomura executives were aware of the payoffs or whether, as the brokerage maintains, the officials involved acted on their own.

Prosecutors are also probing for signs of possible misdeeds linked to so-called "VIP accounts" set up for elite customers including bureaucrats and politicians. Nomura has denied preferential treatment was given to VIP account holders.
Industry sources said prosecutors were also looking into whether other banks had improper dealings with Koike.
A series of scandals this decade has starred the triad of businessmen, gangsters and politicians which emerged with the birth of Japan's political parties in the late 19th century and survives today.

Top Nomura executives Setsuya Tabuchi and Yoshihisa Tabuchi (no relation) and Nikko Securities executives resigned in 1991 after revelations the brokerages compensated favoured clients for losses and had dealings with organised crime.
But the two men stayed as shadow management "shogun" and in 1995 rejoined Nomura's board, to the dismay of many employees.

The 1991 brokerage scandals, combined with loan fraud scams at some of the nation's top banks, forced Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to resign as finance minister and contributed to what some see as a Hashimoto vendetta against Nomura.
Hashimoto has another big reason for wanting to be seen acting tough on financial misdoings -- his push to carry out "Big Bang" reforms to make Tokyo markets globally competitive.
"As they try to internationalise the financial system, they have got to play by world rules and that involves trying to clean up the mess," said one foreign financial analyst.
Prosecutors have reportedly mobilised some 30 investigators for a probe that could last until September.

DKB executives as well as Setsuya Tabuchi and former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki are to be summoned before an Upper House panel on Wednesday and executives from the two financial institutions may have to appear before a Lower House committee as well.
The scandal is dealing a big blow to Nomura's business and proving hugely embarrassing for DKB. It also has Japanese business worried about further damage to its image abroad.
Sceptics, however, are still wary of forecasting that the scandal will spread far enough to rock the upper echelons of Japan's political and bureaucratic establishment.

"The focus is basically coming from the regulators, from the Finance Ministry, which wants to send a strong message that the move toward transparency and accountability is for real," said one foreign economist.
Others have more cynical reasons for predicting the political sideshow to the scandal will fade. "There are simply too many people involved," one political analyst said.
